nameStory: The starlet sea anemone gets its charming name from its tiny size and star-like appearance when viewed from above. When its delicate tentacles are fully extended around its mouth, it resembles a miniature star floating in the brackish waters of salt marshes.
description: The starlet sea anemone is a tiny marine animal that looks like a small flower or star in the water. Unlike the larger, colorful sea anemones you might see in tide pools, this little creature is quite small and translucent, with a slender column-like body that burrows into muddy bottoms. Only its ring of delicate tentacles pokes above the surface, waving gently in the current to catch microscopic prey. It's actually related to corals and jellyfish, all sharing stinging cells called cnidocytes.

idTips.label: Buried column
idTips.description: Look for just the top portion visible above mud - the main body stays hidden below the surface, giving it a 'floating tentacles' appearance

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Count the tentacles carefully - they're arranged in neat rings around a central mouth, typically creating a star-like pattern when fully extended

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small compared to rocky shore anemones - the visible portion is often smaller than a penny and easy to overlook

idTips.label: Water type
idTips.description: Found only in brackish water that tastes slightly salty but not as salty as the open ocean - never in freshwater ponds or fully marine environments

idTips.label: Substrate preference
idTips.description: Always in soft, muddy bottoms that feel squishy underfoot - never attached to rocks or hard surfaces like other anemones

idTips.label: Movement response
idTips.description: Quickly retracts all tentacles when disturbed, disappearing completely into the mud within seconds

habitat: Look for starlet anemones in the shallow, brackish waters of coastal salt marshes and lagoons throughout New England. They prefer muddy, soft-bottomed areas where fresh and salt water mix, often in protected coves and tidal creeks. You'll find them in areas that flood and drain with the tides, buried in the organic-rich mud alongside salt marsh grasses.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, with tentacles more frequently extended for feeding as plankton populations increase.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when tentacles are most visible and extended, making identification easier in the warm brackish waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be less conspicuous as water temperatures drop and feeding activity decreases.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and buried deeper in mud, making winter observation very difficult in New England's cold coastal waters.

funFact: This tiny anemone is actually a scientific superstar - researchers have mapped its entire genetic code, making it one of the most thoroughly studied animals on Earth, yet it's so rare in the wild that it's listed as a vulnerable species!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with small tube worms or baby sea anemones, but starlet anemones are the only ones that live buried in brackish mud with just tentacles showing. Remember: 'Star in the marsh mud' - if it's in salty tide pool rocks, it's probably a different anemone species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sea' anemone, this species actually requires brackish water - the mix of fresh and salt water found in coastal marshes. It can't survive in purely marine or freshwater environments, making it quite specialized compared to its ocean-dwelling relatives.
compareHints: The starlet anemone is actually the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in the region. Compared to other small anemones in the Edwardsiidae family, it's distinguished by its exclusive brackish water habitat and completely buried lifestyle - most other family members attach to hard surfaces or live in fully marine conditions.
